body.text: The federal government’s plan to impose special Australian-designed safety and security standards on artificial intelligence companies has hit a snag. Its own newly published rapid-review report into OpenAI agents’ hacking of a Medicare statistics website contains a warning: unless Australian rules are replicated by other countries they won’t work.

When Anthony Albanese stood in his courtyard at Parliament House on 10 November and promised new legislated standards, he released the review’s eighteen recommendations but not the full thirty-six-page report itself.

“You will get to see the report,” he told journalists querying its absence. When asked why they couldn’t question him on the whole document, he promised to release it at some unspecified time, saying: “We’re protecting our national interest of our national security.”

The report was published on his departmental website last Friday, ten days after he spoke alongside deputy prime minister and defence minister Richard Marles and home affairs minister Tony Burke. It contains further details of a series of incidents which OpenAI didn’t discover until August and didn’t disclose until September. The report reinforces concerns about how the company handled the breaches, and about the gaps they exposed in the government’s cybersecurity response processes. It supports encouraging frontier AI companies to shift the development and training of new, more advanced models to Australia.

“Hosting frontier training infrastructure would give Australia greater opportunity to shape proportionate safety and transparency commitments, while strengthening its voice in emerging international approaches,” says the report.
But preceding that observation is a reality check on the effectiveness of any unilateral attempt to impose Australian standards on the operations of companies headquartered elsewhere.

“Australia will face challenges if it seeks to regulate these systems in isolation,” the report says. “Significant divergence from international approaches could create enforcement difficulties and reduce the practical reach of Australian rules, particularly where firms are able to shift development or deployment activities to jurisdictions with less stringent requirements. This reinforces the importance of international cooperation to support effective regulation and promote shared expectations regarding AI safety and accountability.”

Back in July, in his speech laying out the government’s intended direction on AI, Albanese said Australia could “set the terms” for the technology’s use, applying Australian values to a set of new “Australian standards.” He joined Norway and Finland and what are now twenty-nine other countries in calling for global AI regulation as a matter of urgency.

The rapid review report says domestic regulation “will be strengthened when aligned with international expectations and regulatory approaches.” Any Australian standards, it continues, “should be viewed as complementary elements of a broader framework for managing the risks associated with increasingly capable systems.” As benchmarks, it points to existing regulations in the US state of California and in the European Union.

Albanese’s argument for encouraging frontier companies to move their model training here rests heavily on the assertion that Australia can influence the frontier companies’ safety and security standards. Since the hacking incidents involving OpenAI, the government’s conversations about that possibility are now primarily with Anthropic, creator of the Claude AI product, which is demanding a weakening of copyright law as a condition of moving.

Shifting to an opt-in, opt-out copyright system rather than the licence-based system that now applies would allow the company to much more easily train its models, without charge, on the copyrighted works not only of Australian creative producers but also their worldwide counterparts. An opt-in, opt-out system would undermine creators’ existing automatic licensing rights, requiring writers, artists and musicians to actively agree or disagree to AI companies scanning, or scraping, their work and using it to train increasingly capable software models. Those opting in would receive an unspecified payment. Those declining would be relying on a digital keep-out tag to stop access. Doing neither would also be deemed a choice — to permit access for free.

This system would also apply to works from around the world if the scraping was done from Australia, effectively undermining the system globally. That prospect has prompted a campaign by Australia’s creative industries backed by high-profile musicians and writers overseas, who are urging the government not to sell them out. Albanese has now deferred legislative work on the issue until the new year.

He is flagging more talks on the wide-ranging legal implications of embracing AI, not only for copyright law. “There’s going to be a lot of consultation, and we will undertake that,” Albanese said on Friday, not acknowledging that consultations on copyright have already been extensive but without resolution. “We haven’t landed a final thing of whether there’ll be one piece of legislation or multiples.”
A “range” of existing legislation would require amendment, he added. “In particular, national security legislation. This is very complex.”

The rapid-review report concentrates on cyber security. It reiterates government’s strong concern over OpenAI’s handling of the incidents after discovering its AI agents had hacked into the Medicare site, had tried to hack the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare’s website and had entered several other Australian government sites without authorisation. It confirms that prosecution for the intrusions isn’t possible because current Australian law doesn’t cover the actions of AI software programs acting on their own volition without a human directing the activity.

But it also cautions against relying on undertakings from OpenAI and other companies to more actively monitor agents’ activities during evaluation and training, and report any further incidents urgently, clearly and directly. It suggests that goodwill and promises might not be sufficient to deter the most serious forms of misconduct.

“Governments may therefore need to consider whether criminal penalties are appropriate in cases involving an AI developer having reckless disregard for known risks or serious failures to implement reasonable safeguards,” the report continues. “Criminal penalties may be justified where significant departures from accepted safety obligations create substantial and foreseeable risks of serious harm.”

Albanese has already said he accepts the review’s recommendations and will consider introducing criminal penalties for future breaches. The report emphasises that the impact of the Medicare hack was not serious because it didn’t access confidential information but that it has significant implications for the security of government and other computer systems.

In a move some may find contentious, the review team recommends removing perceived disincentives for AI companies to report incidents by giving them explicit protection from being penalised for their agents’ activities if they disclose them. It says the change should replicate the “limited use” provisions in current intelligence and cybersecurity law that protect other tech companies.

But it also stresses that this cannot become a get-out-of-jail-free provision. “Protections designed to encourage disclosure should not operate as a safe harbour from regulatory scrutiny or accountability,” it says. “Voluntary disclosures and protections analogous to Limited Use provisions may support information sharing, but should not prevent regulators or law enforcement from exercising their own information gathering or enforcement powers.”
In other words, investigators must be able to gather their own evidence separate from the disclosure and take action when warranted.

The report proposes a tiered model of possible new civil and criminal offences, depending on the severity of an incident. It also suggests a standalone “failure to prevent” offence when an AI company doesn’t take reasonable steps to prevent harm.

Within days of the rapid-review report’s release, parliament’s select committee on AI published its 418-page report Artificial Intelligence: The Australian Way, which is subtitled In Our Interest. On Our Terms. The hefty volume is the fruit of the committee’s own rapid inquiry, conducted on a tight government-imposed deadline and under specific terms of reference.

“AI is here, it is in all our lives, and it will continue to evolve whether we choose to play a role in its evolution or not,” the report says. “It is this choice — to involve our nation in the development of the most significant technology of our time — that we must seriously consider. It is a decision that may have far-reaching implications, not least of which for our sovereignty and our national security. However, it is a decision we have agency over — a decision we can make in our interest and on our own terms.”

The inquiry was asked to canvass the broad sweep of AI, from the state of the technology and pace of development to its industry and economic possibilities, its productivity potential and the risk of harm. It examined the requirements and likely impact of the data centres required to run it, and the technology’s implications for cyber and national security, research, education, the workforce, service delivery, the workings of government and online safety. It also looked at the issues around copyright.

The committee’s members came from the Labor, Liberal and Nationals parties, with two independents — Western Australian MP Kate Chaney and independent ACT senator David Pocock. All but Pocock endorsed the report in full.

The thrust of its forty-eight recommendations was foreshadowed in a letter committee which chair and Labor backbencher Jo Briskey and her Liberal deputy (and now former senator) Jonno Duniam wrote to Albanese last month. That letter attracted controversy after metadata revealed it had been created and partially drafted in the prime minister’s office. It’s understood the letter to Albanese was written at his request.

On copyright, the committee’s report was slightly less amenable to the labs’ demands than expected. Although it said the companies “should be doing deals with Australian rightsholders” it also appeared to propose different treatment for smaller rightsholders from those represented by large agencies, associations and publishing houses. It described using rightsholders’ works without permission or payment as “wrong” but confined that criticism to the use of Australians’ works. It also referred to “strengthening” and “improving” copyright law — language the government has used to describe proposed measures the creative industries have argued would do anything but that. The main report is silent on the opt-in, opt-out idea. Only a dissenting report from Pocock described the proposal, and listed who among witnesses to the inquiry were for it and who — in larger numbers — were against.

The music industry has been particularly strident in its opposition. This week, the Australasian Mechanical Copyright Owners Society, which represents those holding the rights to musical works, welcomed the report but repeated concerns about the opt-in, opt-out proposal.

“We’re ready to sit down with the government and with any platform that wants a licence,” chief executive Dean Ormston said. “The prime minister drew the line in July when he said anything less than creators’ control is theft. An opt-out scheme falls on the wrong side of that line. We’re asking the government to hold it: rule out opt-out, legislate full transparency and make the platforms come and get a licence.”

In his lengthy dissenting report, Pocock endorsed much of what the main report proposed but argued that some recommendations should be stronger and opposed acquiescing to the frontier companies on copyright. “We cannot allow Australia to become the copyright equivalent of the Cayman Islands,” his report said.

As the parliamentary year ended, Albanese was still refusing to commit either way or say much more about what he planned to legislate or how his proposed standards would work, telling journalists: “We’ll work those things through.” •
